summary: Friedrich Christian Diez was a linguist who studied at the universities of Giessen (~1811–1813) and Göttingen (~1818–1820). He held a post at the University of Bonn from around 1823 to 1876.

Friedrich Creuzer worked in religious studies, history, archaeology, and philosophy, having studied at Jena (~1789–1791) and Tübingen (~1791–1792). He held academic posts at Marburg (~1800–1804), Heidelberg (~1804–1845), and Leiden (1809).

Friedrich Delitzsch was a scholar of linguistics, history, and archaeology. He studied at Leipzig and Berlin under Fleischer, Brockhaus, Curtius, Dillmann, and Windisch, later holding professorial posts at Breslau (~1893–1899) and Berlin (~1899–1920).

Friedrich Ernst August Krause was a sinologist who studied at the Seminar für Orientalische Sprachen zu Berlin from ~1904 to 1906. He later held a post at the University of Heidelberg from ~1924 to 1940.

Friedrich Haag studied at Zurich under Heinrich Schweizer-Sidler, as well as at Göttingen and Berlin. He taught at Zurich, Tallinn Cathedral School, Kantonsschule Schaffhausen, and Gymnasium Burgdorf before serving as professor of classical philology at Bern (1887; 1891–1906).

Friedrich Heiler was a religious studies scholar who earned his doctorate at the University of Munich (~1912–1917). He taught at Munich (1918) and Marburg (1920), and directed the Religionskundliche Sammlung (~1927–1962).

Windischmann earned doctorates at Bonn (under Christian Lassen, Karl Windischmann, and A. W. von Schlegel) and Munich. He taught at Munich and Lyzeum Freising (1838–1839) before serving as vicar general for the Archdiocese of Munich and Freising (~1846–1861).

Friedrich Hirth was a scholar of sinology, history, and archaeology who studied at Leipzig, Berlin, and Greifswald. He worked for the Chinese Maritime Customs Service (1870–1897) and held the Dean Lung Professorship of Chinese at Columbia University (1902).

Friedrich Leo was a linguist who studied at Göttingen and Bonn, the latter under Hermann Usener. He held academic posts at Bonn, Kiel, Rostock, Strasbourg, and the University of Göttingen (1889–1914).

Friedrich Majer worked in Indology, history, and archaeology. He studied at the University of Jena (~1791–1794) and under Johann Gottfried von Herder (~1796–1803), serving as a Privatdozent at Jena from ~1799 to 1802.

A scholar of Indology, linguistics, and religious studies, Müller studied at Leipzig, Berlin, and under Eugène Burnouf and H. H. Wilson. He spent his career at Oxford, serving as professor of modern European languages and comparative philology.

Friedrich Müller was a linguist and Indologist who studied at Vienna, Göttingen, and Tübingen. He held posts at the Vienna University Library, the Austrian National Library, and served as a professor at the University of Vienna from 1869.

Friedrich Nietzsche worked in philosophy and linguistics, studying at the universities of Bonn and Leipzig, including under Friedrich Ritschl. He served on the faculty at the University of Basel from 1869 to 1878.

Friedrich Otto Schrader was an Indologist and philosopher who earned his doctorate at the University of Strasbourg (~1899–1902). He served as director of the Adyar Library (1905–1916) and became a professor at Kiel University in 1921.
Friedrich Ritschl was a linguist who studied at Leipzig and Halle. He held academic posts at the University of Halle (~1829–1833), Breslau (1834), Bonn (1839), and Leipzig (~1865–1875).

Friedrich Rosen completed his doctoral studies under Franz Bopp (~1824–1826). He subsequently held posts at University College London as professor of Sanskrit (~1828–1837) and at the University of London as professor of Oriental literature (1834).

Friedrich Rückert was a scholar of Indology, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied under Franz Bopp and Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall, later serving as professor at Erlangen (1826) and the University of Berlin (1841–1849).

Friedrich Schlegel was an Indologist, linguist, and philosopher who studied under C. G. Heyne, Alexander Hamilton, and Antoine-Léonard de Chézy. He held posts at the universities of Jena, Cologne, and TU Dresden.

Friedrich Schleiermacher was a philosopher and religious studies scholar who studied at the University of Halle (~1787–1790). He held academic posts at Halle (~1804–1807) and held a chair at the University of Berlin (~1810–1834).

Friedrich Schrader worked in Indology, history, and archaeology. He completed his doctoral dissertation under the supervision of Richard Pischel at the Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg between ~1885 and 1889.
